text: Everything this course has taught — the four dimensions, the Service Value System, the value chain activities, and the practices from Chapters 4 through 6 — is exactly the scope of the real ITIL 4 Foundation certification. Foundation is intentionally broad and shallow: it gives everyone in an ITSM-adjacent role, from a new service desk agent to a seasoned ops manager, the same shared vocabulary. It's the one credential required before any other ITIL 4 exam, and for most platform roles, including ServiceNow roles, it's the only one most people will ever need.

Beyond Foundation, the scheme splits into two tracks. Managing Professional is built for people who design, deliver, and support IT-enabled services day to day — its modules go deeper into execution: planning and running services, measuring and communicating value to stakeholders, and adapting practices for high-velocity delivery. Strategic Leader is aimed at people shaping IT strategy at an organizational level, connecting IT strategy to business strategy rather than day-to-day operations.

One module, Direct, Plan and Improve, is shared by both streams — a required prerequisite covering governance, strategy, and continual improvement. The Strategic Leader stream's other module, Digital and IT Strategy, pushes furthest into genuine business-strategy territory, looking at how digital capability becomes a competitive factor, not just a support function.

ITIL 4 Master sits above both streams, and it isn't earned by sitting one more exam alone — it requires holding both the Managing Professional and Strategic Leader designations, plus demonstrating practical application of ITIL concepts in a real work setting. It's aimed at ITSM leadership and consulting careers specifically, not something most platform practitioners will pursue, and not a near-term goal this early in a career path.

Every level here is assessed through a proctored, multiple-choice exam run by an accredited exam institute, PeopleCert being the most widely used. This course won't guess at an exact question count or passing score — check the current official details from the accrediting body before you sit any real exam. Next: the capstone, putting this whole course to work on one organization.
